thread.title: Gov. candidates talk worker protections in UAW forum
thread.title_full: Gov. candidates talk worker protections in UAW forum

author: Christina Zhang
title: Gov. candidates talk worker protections in UAW forum
text:
Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan and Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson joined the United Auto Workers in Dearborn Monday evening for a gubernatorial forum. Candidates for the Michigan governor’s election took questions from UAW members, focusing on candidates’ plans to support labor unions and prioritize the working class over corporate interests. During the forum, Benson and Duggan sparred over their positions on corporate PAC donations, specifically contributions from DTE Energy.
Republican primary frontrunners U.S. Rep. John James and Perry Johnson were also invited but did not attend.
The UAW is Michigan’s largest labor union, with more than 350,000 active and retired members. Most of its members work in automobile and auto parts industries, as well as in healthcare and higher education.
Each candidate had 90 seconds to deliver an opening statement before taking questions. In Swanson’s opening statement, he highlighted his longstanding American Federation of Teachers membership and his actions as sheriff that built trust with the community.
“There are people in this room — and if I looked in your eyes right now, you know that when you picked up that phone and you called me — I took care of you, your members, your family,” Swanson said.
In her opening statement, Benson said she would stand up for the working class, referencing her efforts as Secretary of State to protect Michigan’s private voter information from the federal government.
“I’ll stand with you on the picket line when you’re fighting for that fair contract, call out corporate greed, stop plant closures and make sure you get the benefits you’re entitled to — whether it’s your health care, your unemployment or your pension — because that’s what government’s supposed to do,” Benson said.
Duggan, who left the Democratic Party in 2024 and is now running as an Independent, centered his opening statement on his experience as mayor of Detroit working with UAW to create jobs. As mayor, Duggan oversaw numerous deals with businesses such as Flex-N-Gate, LM Manufacturing and Lear Corporation to bring manufacturing plants into the city.
“For 12 years, I have worked with you and Jimmy Settles to put the Flex-N-Gate plant on St. Cyril, to put the Lear plant on Connor, to put the Dakota plant on Van Dyke, to put the LM seating plant on Fort Street,” Duggan said. “I’m not here to talk about what I’m going to do, but talk about what we’ve done together.”
UAW local union members then stepped up to ask questions. When asked whether corporate interests will have more influence in candidates’ policies than those of working families, both Benson and Swanson said they have not taken corporate PAC money.
“I have not taken a dime of corporate PAC money in my campaign, because I think the fundamental question that’s going to be facing voters this year is ‘Who does your governor work for?’” Benson said. “I will work for you, not the highest bidder, not a lobbyist, not Donald Trump.”
Duggan, who has been transparent about accepting corporate PAC donations, said he hopes to bridge the gap between business and labor, and represent both corporate and worker interests. He criticized Benson for accepting a $1.5 million contribution in 2024 from Ken Duda that went toward Benson’s own Michigan Legacy PAC.
“You took a $1.5 million contribution from Ken Duda, the man who builds the data warehouses and connects them across America,” Duggan said. “$1.5 million personal contribution into that PAC and then you come in and say, ‘Sorry, I don’t take a $10,000 corporate check.’”
Benson then fired back at Duggan in response to a question about prioritizing workers over corporate incentives, citing a lack of transparency in Duggan’s campaign donations.
“Mr. Duggan, you’ve up until now refused to say who’s funding the several dark money accounts that are putting out millions of dollars in ads for your campaign, but I hope you’ll tell us who the highest donors are to those now,” Benson said.
When asked about the potential for artificial intelligence technologies to put jobs at risk, the candidates responded with their plans to implement guardrails so data centers can be built in the interest of community and environmental concerns.
“I also have established a data center incorporation plan, where any type of corporation or data center is coming to Michigan,” Benson said. “We welcome the well-paying union jobs that they could bring, but we have to put guardrails in place to ensure they don’t use and abuse our natural resources, that they commit to driving down energy costs.”
A local union member asked about DTE’s increasing utility rates, inviting candidates to disclose whether they take DTE money.
Both Swanson and Benson stated they do not take donations from DTE. Benson highlighted her intended energy affordability plan, which she says will end unfair, profit-driven rate hikes and build clean energy infrastructure.
Duggan responded by consulting ChatGPT about Benson previously accepting campaign donations from DTE while running for Secretary of State.
“Maybe ChatGPT has it wrong, but it says the state finance records of Jocelyn Benson show that she accepted DTE PAC checks in her 2010 and 2018 campaigns,” Duggan said. “At some point you have to have an honest conversation. When you discover your values in the middle of an election, when electric rates are soaring, at some point, we’ve got to talk about what … we say we do and what … we do.”
In response to a question about voting accessibility, Benson criticized Duggan for seeking help on writing policy from Gerry Anderson, former chairman and CEO of DTE.
“I don’t know who’s influencing who here, but I think when the facts are played out, we’ll see exactly where the money is and who is actually influencing other candidates on this stage, and it’s not me,” Benson said.
Duggan claimed he was proud to have the support of Anderson because it aligns with his goal of connecting corporate and worker interests.
The candidates were all in favor of protecting reproductive rights, fighting against U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement overreach and expanding unemployment benefits to striking workers.
Duggan previously served as president and CEO of the Detroit Medical Center before running for mayor of Detroit. He drew criticism from an audience member for alleged union busting when he was CEO and receiving money from anti-union donors. Duggan defended himself by highlighting the DMC’s growth over his tenure and his numerous gubernatorial campaign endorsements from labor unions.
Managing News Editor Christina Zhang can be reached at zchristi@umich.edu.
summary: Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan and Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson joined the United Auto Workers in Dearborn Monday evening for a gubernatorial forum. In her opening statement, Benson said she would stand up for the working class, referencing her efforts as Secretary of State to protect Michigan’s private voter information from the federal government.
